newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Korean firms not doing enough in Malaysia - report.
newsitem.headline: Korean firms not doing enough in Malaysia - report.

text.p: A Malaysian business leader accused South Korean firms of not doing enough to justify their infrastructure contracts in the Southeast Asian nation, Bernama news agency reported on Thursday.
Adam Harun, vice-president of the National Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Malaysia (NCCIM), said South Korean companies do not transfer technology to Malaysian companies.

Adam, speaking at a luncheon hosted in honour of visiting South Korean Deputy Prime Minister Han Seung-Soo, said South Korean companies preferred farming out small contracts in major deals in Malaysia to their own national firms.
South Korean companies were also found to be not making much investment in high-technology in Malaysia, Adam said.
"Thus, we, the Malaysian private sector would propose that such practices be stopped so as not to affect the strong and good ties between the two countries," Adam was quoted as saying by Bernama.
Han, on a two-day visit to Malaysia, did not comment.
Big projects clinched by South Koreans in Malaysia include the Petronas Twin Towers, said to be the tallest buildings in the world. Samsung Engineering and Construction Co built one of the towers.

Meanwhile, at news conference on Thursday, Han said Seoul had no plans to slow down on foreign investment or discourage luxurious lifestyles despite South Korea having one of its worst economic cycles this year.

"We are in the process of rewriting the foreign investment law, that will contain elements of liberalisation in our economy," Han said, as he dismissed possibilities of the government tightening capital outflow for investment.
"It's also the policy of the government not to interfere too much in the consumption behaviour of the people," he said.

Han said a huge fall in exports growth and prices, due largely to the depreciation of the Japanese yen, had made 1996 a difficult year, with gross domestic product growth being revised down from 7.8 per cent to seven percent.

Han's visit did not yield any new deals between the two countries. But the deputy premier, in his talks with Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, urged the strong trade and investment ties between the two nations to continue.
Han said bilateral trade jumped 55 percent to $5.5 billion in 1995. He said South Korean firms poured $1.2 billion into 110 projects in Malaysia between 1991 and 1995.
